title: Harbor Phase Works
summary: One multipaneled opening comic page establishes Harbor Phase as a functioning, automated coastal city and Matt as a man positioned near responsibility without much agency. The page moves from city scale to transit to municipal oversight to ordinary managed public life.

panelPlan.text: Wide opening panel: rain over functioning Harbor Phase—elevated transit, floodwalls, automated freight and calm civic systems. The city is efficient, not ruined.
Matt rides elevated transit above the floodwall while the system reroutes minor tidal flooding before passengers need to react.
Municipal control room: drainage obstruction is detected, a drone crew handles it, and Matt is asked only for human confirmation.
Closer on Matt and the interface; his work still uses the language of responsibility even when the meaningful decision is already finished.
Matt exits into pleasant managed Harbor Phase: wet glass, civic lighting, continuity-payment messaging, and ordinary people moving through a city that absorbs inconvenience for them.

dialogueInline.speaker: SYSTEM
dialogueInline.text: Minor tidal flooding downtown. Route adjusted.

dialogueInline.speaker: SYSTEM
dialogueInline.text: Drainage obstruction detected. Drone crew dispatched.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: His job still used the language of responsibility.

dialogueInline.speaker: SCREEN
dialogueInline.text: Your Continuity Payment posts tomorrow. Harbor Phase thanks you for participating.

directionInline.text: Prestige indie sequential page; varied panel scale from civic establishing shot to intimate close-up. Humane optimized comfort, not apocalypse. No page header or production labels.

title: Managed Adulthood
summary: One multipaneled ensemble montage shows five friends living materially stable lives that barely require their judgment: Chris reviews machine-made software, Ryan repairs old marine equipment, Kevin watches automated risk systems, Justin burns energy in optimized training, and Nicole finds an old Sector 14 expansion clipping that looks wrong enough to keep.

panelPlan.text: Chris at a screen reviewing an already-verified automated software patch; his human approval is ceremonial.
Ryan in a small marine workshop ignores a system recommendation and repairs old equipment by feel.
Kevin studies a tide/risk display whose automated language understates what bothers him.
Justin finishes an optimized training session and receives an instantly generated recovery protocol; he is unimpressed.
Nicole at a table with an old Harbor Phase expansion clipping/printout marked SECTOR 14; she keeps looking because the geography does not sit right.
Closing montage beat links their separate lives visually through rain, screens, old tools and underused human attention.

dialogueInline.speaker: DISPLAY
dialogueInline.text: Performance percentile: 96. Recommended recovery protocol generated.

directionInline.text: Five distinct adult lives on one page. Preserve clear character differences and avoid making the montage feel like a dossier or labeled contact sheet.

title: Nobody Leaves
summary: One multipaneled bar scene establishes the adult friend-group rhythm, Chris's observation that nobody really leaves anymore, and the moment Reach rumors turn a familiar night into a decision. Runner messages and the old group chat pull all six toward the same low-tide window.

panelPlan.text: Wide bar panel: all six friends in a comfortable, rain-darkened Harbor Phase bar, already talking over one another with old familiarity.
Smaller conversational panels carry the rescue-cert joke and Chris's thought that nobody actually leaves anymore.
Reaction panels keep the exchange adult and lived-in rather than theatrical: skepticism, irritation, amusement and recognition.
Phones/devices light up with runner-channel chatter about the outer shelf and Sector 14.
The group chat lands the practical question: are they going tonight?
Final group beat: the joking stops just enough for everyone to understand that they are going.

dialogueInline.speaker: Justin Rourke
dialogueInline.text: I’m saying physically I could have passed the rescue cert.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kevin Marsh
dialogueInline.text: Physical is usually where you start losing arguments.

dialogueInline.speaker: Chris Barlow
dialogueInline.text: You ever notice nobody actually leaves anymore?

dialogueInline.speaker: Nicole Hanley
dialogueInline.text: I thought Sector 14 stopped before the wall.

directionInline.text: Keep the bar warm but emotionally flat compared with the outside rain. Natural adult ensemble acting; no character-name labels or scene title on the page.

title: Floodwall
summary: One multipaneled threshold page takes the group from gear preparation through the old ferry lot and onto the exposed seabed. Runner culture is practical and unofficial; Ryan reads the water, Matt tries to organize, Chris is underprepared, Justin jokes, Nicole participates, Kevin worries, and the tide window becomes physical.

panelPlan.text: Wide ferry-lot establishing panel: open trunks, cheap gear, runner clusters, floodwall mass, wet pavement, tide board, contractor work lights and vehicle headlights.
Matt finds Chris with a barely charged scanner; their old rhythm is immediate.
Justin floats a casino rumor while Nicole and Matt dismiss it from inside the joke.
Ryan checks Chris's footwear and makes the trench risk concrete.
Ryan and Kevin compare the changed north crossing against the public model; Ryan trusts water over the model.
A low siren and movement through the staging area push everyone toward the flood steps.
Final wide panel: the six descend from the floodwall and step onto black exposed seabed. It feels like work, not heroism.

dialogueInline.speaker: TIDE BOARD
dialogueInline.text: LOW WINDOW: 4 HRS 12 MIN. CROSSING CONDITIONS: STABLE. OUTER SHELF EXPOSURE: HIGH.

dialogueInline.speaker: Chris Barlow
dialogueInline.text: Spiritually, it’s at one hundred percent.

dialogueInline.speaker: Justin Rourke
dialogueInline.text: Okay. I’m hearing there’s a casino out there.

dialogueInline.speaker: Matt Donnelly
dialogueInline.text: There is not a casino out there.

dialogueInline.speaker: Ryan Kelleher
dialogueInline.text: North crossing shifted after the storms.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kevin Marsh
dialogueInline.text: That is not in the public model.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The beginning of the crossing never felt heroic.

directionInline.text: Practical light only: headlamps, cheap LEDs, phone/scanner screens, contractor work lights and vehicle lights. No lanterns. Preserve the six-character identity models established by approved production art.

title: The First Mile
summary: One multipaneled crossing page makes the first mile bodily and ugly: mud suction, shells, fishing line, cold pools and distance. The six stop looking like urban explorers and start looking like people doing difficult physical work together.

panelPlan.text: Wide panel: the six small against the floodwall and a huge black tidal flat, practical lights receding behind them.
Close inserts: boots sinking, shell crunch, fishing line, shallow cold water and mud pulling at each step.
Midshot of the group recalibrating to the physical discomfort; clothes and gear are wet and dirty now.
Chris admits the crossing is worse than memory; Ryan answers without drama.
Long closing panel: they keep moving into fog, Harbor Phase dimming behind them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Chris Barlow
dialogueInline.text: This is always worse than I remember.

directionInline.text: Physical cold and difficult footing must read clearly. Keep the page grounded and unsentimental; no heroic expedition posing.

title: Walking Rhythm
summary: One multipaneled page settles into the crossing rhythm. Matt checks the tide monitor too often, Chris needles him, Justin drifts toward performance, Kevin voices the risk, and Ryan dryly predicts Justin will survive long enough to become unbearable. Nicole remains part of the moving group rather than a commentator outside it.

panelPlan.text: Wide rear/side view of all six walking the flats in a staggered line, headlamps and wet clothing catching practical light.
Matt checks the tide monitor again while Chris notices.
Chris and Matt trade the joke while continuing to walk; nobody stops for a speech.
Justin moves with more energy than the group, testing footing and attention.
Kevin watches him and voices what the others are thinking.
Ryan answers with dry certainty; final panel returns to the group moving forward through black water and fog.

dialogueInline.speaker: Chris Barlow
dialogueInline.text: You checking that every thirty seconds helps the ocean respect you more?

dialogueInline.speaker: Matt Donnelly
dialogueInline.text: It helps me respect me more.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kevin Marsh
dialogueInline.text: Guy’s gonna get himself swept one night.

dialogueInline.speaker: Ryan Kelleher
dialogueInline.text: He’ll probably survive long enough to become unbearable first.

directionInline.text: Preserve immediate costume/gear wetness and the exact approved six-person visual identity. The previous page may guide carried state but is not the sole identity reference.

title: The Wrong Way
summary: One multipaneled discovery page moves from mud onto old pavement. Road markings point in the wrong direction for shoreline access, and the group begins to understand that the geometry ahead is larger and more organized than rumor suggested. Fog gives them only fragments of what is coming.

panelPlan.text: The six reach an old paved strip emerging from mud; faded road paint and drainage details change the texture of the crossing.
Nicole crouches or looks closely at the markings while Chris jokes and Matt asks what matters.
Nicole points out that the markings run the wrong way; her observation is concrete and participatory, not a lecture.
The group looks ahead as a hard vertical edge appears through fog.
Fragment panels: another line, a massive support, reflected practical light—enough to imply scale without revealing it.
Final panel lets fog swallow the shape again as Chris's awe turns briefly to fear.

directionInline.text: The visual reveal carries the meaning. Do not make Nicole an exposition device. Practical lights and fog only; no supernatural glow.

title: First Sight
summary: One multipaneled chapter-ending page confirms Sector 14 and then reveals the Reach at full scale. Foundations, transit fragments and a damaged sign prove this was organized city expansion; Justin is thrilled, the others slow down, and the last wide image makes the six tiny between Harbor Phase and an unfinished offshore future.

panelPlan.text: Damaged Sector 14 sign and concrete/transit fragments emerge from the flats; the human intent of the place is undeniable.
Kevin and Nicole react to how far offshore construction actually extended.
Justin returns or surges forward, shaken and delighted by the scale.
The group keeps walking as towers and an elevated structure resolve one piece at a time through fog.
Reaction strip: awe, caution, fear and excitement distributed across the six without turning them into heroic poses.

Large final panel/splash: the Reach—vast unfinished offshore district, wet concrete and black water, the six tiny in foreground, Harbor Phase dim behind. The future was built and then simply never inhabited.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kevin Marsh
dialogueInline.text: They built way farther out than people said.

dialogueInline.speaker: Chris Barlow
dialogueInline.text: You ever get the feeling we’re walking somewhere people weren’t supposed to come back from?

dialogueInline.speaker: Ryan Kelleher
dialogueInline.text: Pretty sure that’s the whole point.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: What they had imagined as drowned outskirts was something else.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: A future interrupted before anyone could live in it.

directionInline.text: End Chapter 1 with scale and grounded physical reality. The Reach is fixed abandoned geography, not supernatural. No title card or non-scripted page labels.
